text: A school supply drive can have plenty of donations, and still run short of complete kits.
One group needs crayons. Another needs calculators. Both need notebooks. And some kits were promised weeks ago.
KitBridge answers two questions for the volunteers who pack them. How many complete kits can we make right now? And what should we buy next?
Everything lives on one drive sheet: what's on hand, what goes into each kit, and what a restock pack costs.
The answer sits on top. Stock on hand packs eight kits. With a ten dollar budget, it's twelve of sixteen.
And it explains why. Notebooks and calculators run out first, and one five dollar pack of notebooks adds four kits.
Change any number, and the plan updates as you type. Let's drop the budget to four dollars.
A calculator would fit that budget, but it wouldn't finish a single extra kit. So KitBridge spends nothing.
Promises are hard limits. With only seven backpacks, eight promised kits can't be packed.
KitBridge names the shortage, instead of quietly breaking a promise.
When the plan looks right, open the packing sheets. Pack now from stock, or after the restock arrives.
Each kit type gets a checklist with exact totals, ready to print for the packing table.
It works on a phone too, so the count can happen right in the stockroom.
Under the hood, KitBridge solves a two step integer program with the HiGHS solver, compiled to WebAssembly and running in a web worker.
Step one finds the most complete kits within stock, budget and promises. Step two finds the cheapest purchase that reaches that total.
Money is counted in whole cents, the solver is checked against brute force on ninety six small drives, and nothing ever leaves your device.
Equal access to education starts with a complete kit.
KitBridge. From donated supplies, to complete kits.
